report:
The evidence is more mixed than a simple "yes."

**Earlier meta-analyses (mostly positive):** Older Cochrane reviews, the Allen et al. and Van Niel et al. meta-analyses, and the Lancet meta-analysis by Sazawal et al. reported that probiotics (especially *Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG* and *Saccharomyces boulardii*) modestly shortened diarrhea duration—typically by about 24 hours—and reduced stool frequency, mainly in children in high-income settings (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473309906704959/fulltext).

**Updated Cochrane review (2020, more cautious):** The most recent, high-quality Cochrane systematic review (Collinson et al., 2020) concluded that "probiotics may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts. We do not know if they can shorten the time to recovery," reflecting downgraded confidence due to heterogeneity, small/low-quality trials, and publication bias (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub4/full; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea).

**Large, rigorous RCTs (negative):** Two large, well-conducted, multicenter North American trials published together in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (2018) found that probiotics (*L. rhamnosus GG* alone or combined with *L. helveticus*) did NOT reduce disease severity or duration in children with acute gastroenteritis seen in emergency departments, compared with placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597; https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598).

**Conclusion:** Older, smaller trials (many in developing countries) suggested modest benefit, but larger, more rigorous recent RCTs and updated systematic reviews in high-income settings show no clear benefit. Effectiveness may be strain-, dose-, and population-specific rather than a universal effect—so the current best evidence does not strongly support "yes" as a definitive answer.
